claim: B16ρ0 cells injected into syngeneic C57BL/6Nsu9-DsRed2 mice acquire mtDNA by transfer of whole mitochondria from the host animal.
source: To determine whether the transfer of mtDNA involves whole mitochondria, we injected B16ρ0 mouse melanoma cells into syngeneic C57BL/6Nsu9-DsRed2 mice that express red fluorescent protein in their mitochondria. We document that mtDNA is acquired by transfer of whole mitochondria from the host animal, leading to normalisation of mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, supported by experimental data from the transgenic mouse model described in the manuscript.

claim: Transfer of whole mitochondria from host to B16ρ0 cells leads to normalization of mitochondrial respiration.
source: We document that mtDNA is acquired by transfer of whole mitochondria from the host animal, leading to normalisation of mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this causal relationship, supported by respiration measurements shown in the manuscript.

claim: Knockdown of NDUFV1 in B16ρ0 cells abolished or significantly retarded their ability to form tumours.
source: Additionally, knockdown of key mitochondrial complex I (NDUFV1) and complex II (SDHC) subunits by shRNA in B16ρ0 cells abolished or significantly retarded their ability to form tumours.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by tumor formation data in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown of SDHC in B16ρ0 cells abolished or significantly retarded their ability to form tumours.
source: Additionally, knockdown of key mitochondrial complex I (NDUFV1) and complex II (SDHC) subunits by shRNA in B16ρ0 cells abolished or significantly retarded their ability to form tumours.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by tumor formation data in Figure 3E.

claim: Intact mitochondria with their mtDNA payload are transferred in the developing tumour.
source: Collectively, these results show that intact mitochondria with their mtDNA payload are transferred in the developing tumour, and provide functional evidence for an essential role of oxidative phosphorylation in cancer.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation plays an essential role in cancer.
source: Collectively, these results show that intact mitochondria with their mtDNA payload are transferred in the developing tumour, and provide functional evidence for an essential role of oxidative phosphorylation in cancer.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the knockdown experiments and tumor formation data.

claim: Many human diseases, including cancer, are characterised by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).
source: Many human diseases, including cancer, are characterised by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Cancer cells are more glycolytic than their non-malignant counterparts, as postulated almost a century ago by Warburg.
source: This is linked to altered mitochondrial bioenergetics, such that cancer cells are more glycolytic than their non-malignant counterparts, as postulated almost a century ago by Warburg.
evidence: This refers to the Warburg hypothesis, which is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Altered energy metabolism is regarded as one of the hallmarks of cancer.
source: Altered energy metabolism is now regarded as one of the hallmarks of cancer (Koppenol et al., 2011; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Vyas et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The mitochondrial genome plays a role in tumorigenesis.
source: In this context, the mitochondrial genome has been reported to play a role in tumorigenesis (Lee and St John, 2016; Patananan et al., 2016) and in metastatic cancer (Ishikawa et al., 2008; Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mitochondrial genome plays a role in metastatic cancer.
source: In this context, the mitochondrial genome has been reported to play a role in tumorigenesis (Lee and St John, 2016; Patananan et al., 2016) and in metastatic cancer (Ishikawa et al., 2008; Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cancer cells need oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for their 'pathophysiological' requirements.
source: Although many cancer cells are biased towards the glycolytic metabolism, they also need oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for their 'pathophysiological' requirements (Weinberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weinberg et al., 2010.

claim: Respiration is important for cancer cell proliferation, tumor formation, progression and metastasis.
source: A novel paradigm has emerged, according to which respiration is important for cancer cell proliferation, and also for tumour formation, progression and metastasis (LeBleu et al., 2014; Viale et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to LeBleu et al., 2014 and Viale et al., 2014.

claim: The importance of respiration in cancer is probably linked to metabolic re-modelling.
source: This is probably linked to metabolic re-modelling (Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Some cancer cells retain OXPHOS capacity and have no obvious respiratory defects.
source: There are reports that some cancer cells retain OXPHOS capacity and have no obvious respiratory defects (Frezza and Gottlieb, 2009; Jose et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibiting glycolysis may restore higher rates of OXPHOS in neoplastic cells.
source: Further, inhibiting glycolysis may restore higher rates of OXPHOS in neoplastic cells (Moreno-Sánchez et al., 2007; Michelakis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Depriving cancer cells of their capacity to respire may preclude them from forming tumours.
source: Hence, depriving cancer cells of their capacity to respire may preclude them from forming tumours.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the preceding discussion in the introduction.

claim: Cancer cells without mtDNA (ρ0 cells) form tumours after a considerable delay compared to their parental counterparts.
source: We showed that cancer cells without mtDNA (ρ0 cells) form tumours after a considerable delay compared to their parental counterparts.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work (Tan et al., 2015).

claim: Tumour progression from ρ0 cells was associated with mtDNA acquisition from the host, resulting in respiration recovery.
source: Tumour progression was associated with mtDNA acquisition from the host, resulting in respiration recovery.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous work (Tan et al., 2015).

claim: The homoplasmic polymorphism at the tRNAArg locus of mtDNA in B16ρ0SC cells is of host origin.
source: The assay is able to detect heteroplasmy down to 0.5%, demonstrating with very high confidence that the mtDNA in B16ρ0SC cells is of host origin, and that original B16 polymorphism is either completely absent or present below the detection limit of 0.5% of mtDNA (Figure 1A; see also Appendix 1—figure 1 for validation of sc/ddPCR).
evidence: This is supported by sc/ddPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: B16ρ0 cells lack mtDNA.
source: Appendix 1–figure 2A documents confocal microscopy analysis of mtDNA in mitochondria, showing that B16ρ0 cells lack mtDNA, whereas mtDNA appears homogeneously distributed in mitochondria in all other sub-lines.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Appendix 1-figure 2A.

claim: mtDNA appears homogeneously distributed in mitochondria in B16, B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells.
source: Appendix 1–figure 2A documents confocal microscopy analysis of mtDNA in mitochondria, showing that B16ρ0 cells lack mtDNA, whereas mtDNA appears homogeneously distributed in mitochondria in all other sub-lines.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Appendix 1-figure 2A.

claim: B16, B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells show similar levels and distribution of mtDNA nucleoids.
source: Super-resolution stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy exerted similar levels and distribution of mtDNA nucleoids in B16, B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells, and no nucleoids in B16ρ0 cells, also showing largely unchanged levels of Tom20 and low level of TFAM (Figure 1B; see also Appendix 1—figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: B16ρ0 cells do not contain the supercomplex/respirasome (formed by CI, CIII and CIV).
source: Native blue gel electrophoresis (NBGE) revealed that B16ρ0 cells do not contain the supercomplex/respirasome (formed by CI, CIII and CIV), but contain low amounts of sub-CV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by NBGE data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: B16ρ0 cells contain low amounts of sub-CV.
source: Native blue gel electrophoresis (NBGE) revealed that B16ρ0 cells do not contain the supercomplex/respirasome (formed by CI, CIII and CIV), but contain low amounts of sub-CV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by NBGE data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CII is fully assembled in all B16 sub-lines.
source: CII was found to be fully assembled in all sub-lines, which is reasonable considering that all four subunits in CII are encoded by nuclear DNA (nDNA) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by NBGE data in Figure 1C and is consistent with the fact that CII subunits are nDNA-encoded.

claim: All four subunits in CII are encoded by nuclear DNA (nDNA).
source: CII was found to be fully assembled in all sub-lines, which is reasonable considering that all four subunits in CII are encoded by nuclear DNA (nDNA) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the genetic encoding of CII subunits.

claim: B16, B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells show high levels of DNA polymerase-γ1 (POLG1) binding to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA.
source: This showed a high level of DNA polymerase-γ1 (POLG1) binding to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA in all cells except B16ρ0 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by mitoChIP assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: B16ρ0 cells show no POLG1 binding to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA.
source: This showed a high level of DNA polymerase-γ1 (POLG1) binding to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA in all cells except B16ρ0 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by mitoChIP assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells show similar respiration to B16 cells.
source: B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells showed similar respiration to B16 cells, but no respiration was observed with B16ρ0 cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by respiration measurements shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: No respiration was observed with B16ρ0 cells.
source: B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells showed similar respiration to B16 cells, but no respiration was observed with B16ρ0 cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by respiration measurements shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: B16ρ0 cells produce more lactate than other B16 sub-lines.
source: Accordingly, B16ρ0 cells produced more lactate (Figure 1G) and less ATP (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by lactate production data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: B16ρ0 cells produce less ATP than other B16 sub-lines.
source: Accordingly, B16ρ0 cells produced more lactate (Figure 1G) and less ATP (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by ATP level data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: B16ρ0 cells have lower succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity than other B16 sub-lines.
source: B16ρ0 cells also had lower succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) (Figure 1I) and succinate quinone reductase (SQR) (Figure 1J) activity, as well as lower citrate synthase (CS) activity (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by SDH activity data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: B16ρ0 cells have lower succinate quinone reductase (SQR) activity than other B16 sub-lines.
source: B16ρ0 cells also had lower succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) (Figure 1I) and succinate quinone reductase (SQR) (Figure 1J) activity, as well as lower citrate synthase (CS) activity (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by SQR activity data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: B16ρ0 cells have lower citrate synthase (CS) activity than other B16 sub-lines.
source: B16ρ0 cells also had lower succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) (Figure 1I) and succinate quinone reductase (SQR) (Figure 1J) activity, as well as lower citrate synthase (CS) activity (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by CS activity data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: B16ρ0 and B16ρ0SC cells show higher glucose uptake than B16 cells.
source: Finally, we observed higher glucose uptake in B16ρ0 and B16ρ0SC cells, and lower uptake in B16ρ0SCL cells (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is supported by glucose uptake data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: B16ρ0SCL cells show lower glucose uptake than B16 cells.
source: Finally, we observed higher glucose uptake in B16ρ0 and B16ρ0SC cells, and lower uptake in B16ρ0SCL cells (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is supported by glucose uptake data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Mitochondrial function is fully restored in cells derived from the primary tumour (B16ρ0SC cells).
source: Collectively, these results document that mitochondrial function is already fully restored in cells derived from the primary tumour.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the respiration, enzyme activity, and NBGE data presented in Figure 1.

claim: B16ρ0 cells contain no mtDNA.
source: Appendix 1—figure 2B shows no mtDNA in B16ρ0 cells, while mtDNA was present at similar levels in other sub-lines.
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 1-figure 2B.

claim: mtDNA is present at similar levels in B16, B16ρ0SC, B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells.
source: Appendix 1—figure 2B shows no mtDNA in B16ρ0 cells, while mtDNA was present at similar levels in other sub-lines.
evidence: This is supported by data in Appendix 1-figure 2B.

claim: No mtDNA-encoded transcripts are present in B16ρ0 cells.
source: No mtDNA-encoded transcripts were present in B16ρ0 cells.
evidence: This is stated based on transcript analysis, consistent with the absence of mtDNA in these cells.

claim: mtDNA-encoded transcript levels are low in B16ρ0SC cells.
source: Their levels were low in B16ρ0SC cells, while higher levels were seen for most transcripts in B16ρ0CTC and in B16ρ0SCL cells.
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis data.

claim: Higher levels of mtDNA-encoded transcripts are seen in B16ρ0CTC and B16ρ0SCL cells.
source: Their levels were low in B16ρ0SC cells, while higher levels were seen for most transcripts in B16ρ0CTC and in B16ρ0SCL cells.
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis data.

claim: SCAFI transcripts are present at similar levels in all B16 sub-lines.
source: Transcripts of the assembly factor SCAFI were present at similar levels in all sub-lines, but TFAM transcripts were low in B16ρ0 cells relative to the other cells.
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis data.

claim: TFAM transcripts are low in B16ρ0 cells relative to other B16 sub-lines.
source: Transcripts of the assembly factor SCAFI were present at similar levels in all sub-lines, but TFAM transcripts were low in B16ρ0 cells relative to the other cells.
evidence: This is based on transcript analysis data.

claim: LC3AII levels are lower in B16ρ0 cells, indicating stalled autophagy.
source: WB revealed that most proteins investigated were relatively abundant in all sub-lines with LC3AII levels lower in B16ρ0 cells, indicating stalled autophagy (Appendix 1—figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data in Appendix 1-figure 2C, with interpretation about autophagy.

claim: Many nDNA-encoded mitochondrial proteins, including subunits of respiratory complexes, are unstable in B16ρ0 cells.
source: Interestingly, although present in B16ρ0 cells, many nDNA-encoded mitochondrial proteins, including subunits of RCs, were unstable in these cells, as evidenced using cycloheximide treatment (Appendix 1—figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide treatment data in Appendix 1-figure 2D.

claim: SDHA and ATPβ are stable in B16ρ0 cells, unlike other nDNA-encoded mitochondrial proteins.
source: Exceptions were SDHA and ATPβ; a plausible reason is the absence of binding partners encoded by mtDNA, which could render the 'unassembled nDNA-encoded' subunits unstable.
evidence: This is based on cycloheximide treatment data, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The respiratory function of B16 sublines is fully recovered at the primary tumour stage, in contrast to 4T1 cells.
source: In summary, these results indicate that, in contrast to 4T1 cells (Tan et al., 2015), the respiratory function of B16 sublines is already fully recovered at the primary tumour stage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing B16 and 4T1 cells, based on data in the manuscript and previous work.

claim: All B16 sub-lines except B16ρ0 cells form tumours without delay.
source: We found that all sub-lines formed tumours without delay except for B16ρ0 cells with >2 week delay (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: B16ρ0 cells form tumours with >2 week delay compared to other B16 sub-lines.
source: We found that all sub-lines formed tumours without delay except for B16ρ0 cells with >2 week delay (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tumours derived from all five B16 sub-lines are melanomas with necrotic cells away from blood vessels.
source: Sectioning of tumours derived from all five sub-lines revealed melanomas with necrotic cells away from blood vessels (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on histological examination shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tumours derived from B16ρ0 cells show somewhat higher levels of the respirasome than tumours from other B16 sub-lines.
source: Tumours derived from the sub-lines were assessed by NBGE, identifying full assembly of all complexes as well as the respirasome, with somewhat higher levels of the respirasome in tumours derived from B16ρ0 cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by NBGE data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Tumours derived from B16ρ0 and B16ρ0SCL cells show increased CI-dependent respiration compared to tumours from B16 cells.
source: Figure 2F reveals increased CI-dependent respiration and the maximum electron transfer capacity (ETS) in tumours derived from B16ρ0 and from B16ρ0SCL cells, and no change in CII-dependent respiration.
evidence: This is supported by respiration measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Tumours derived from B16ρ0 and B16ρ0SCL cells show increased maximum electron transfer capacity (ETS) compared to tumours from B16 cells.
source: Figure 2F reveals increased CI-dependent respiration and the maximum electron transfer capacity (ETS) in tumours derived from B16ρ0 and from B16ρ0SCL cells, and no change in CII-dependent respiration.
evidence: This is supported by respiration measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Normal liver tissue from mice grafted with B16 sub-lines shows no changes in respiration.
source: Normal liver tissue from the same animals used as internal control showed no changes in respiration.
evidence: This is based on respiration measurements of liver tissue.

claim: The restoration of tumorigenic potential fully correlates with the observed recovery of respiration.
source: The restoration of the tumorigenic potential fully correlates with the observed recovery of respiration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tumor formation and respiration data.

claim: NDUFV1 KD and SDHC KD cells proliferate at a slower rate than parental B16 cells.
source: Both NDUFV1 KD and SDHC KD cells proliferated at a slower rate than parental cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NDUFV1 KD and SDHC KD cells show lower routine respiration and lower ETS than parental cells.
source: NDUFV1 KD as well as SDHC KD cells showed lower routine respiration and lower ETS (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by respiration data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NDUFV1 KD cells respire less via CI, while CII-dependent respiration is largely unaffected.
source: NDUFV1 KD cells respired less via CI, while CII-dependent respiration was largely unaffected; SDHC KD cells not only showed much lower CII-dependent respiration, but also significantly suppressed CI-dependent respiration (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by respiration data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SDHC KD cells show much lower CII-dependent respiration and significantly suppressed CI-dependent respiration.
source: NDUFV1 KD cells respired less via CI, while CII-dependent respiration was largely unaffected; SDHC KD cells not only showed much lower CII-dependent respiration, but also significantly suppressed CI-dependent respiration (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by respiration data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 4 out of 6 mice grafted with B16ρ0 SDHC KD cells formed tumours with delays of 15 to 40 days compared to B16ρ0 cells.
source: 4 out of 6 mice grafted with B16ρ0 SDHC KD cells formed tumours with delays of 15 to 40 days compared to B16ρ0 cells.
evidence: This is based on tumor formation data from the mouse grafting experiment.

claim: Only one out of 5 mice grafted with B16ρ0 NDUFV1 KD cells formed a tumour, with a lag of about 40 days compared to B16ρ0 cells.
source: Only one out of 5 mice of the B16ρ0 NDUFV1 KD group formed a tumour, with a lag of about 40 days compared to B16ρ0 cells.
evidence: This is based on tumor formation data from the mouse grafting experiment.

claim: B16 NDUFV1 KD and B16 SDHC KD cells show a similar pattern of delayed tumor formation as their B16ρ0 counterparts, though the lag is considerably shorter.
source: A similar pattern was observed for B16 cells and their NDUFV1 KD and SDHC KD variants, though the lag for these sub-lines was considerably shorter (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on tumor formation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: B16 melanoma cells in control tumours show prominent nuclear pleomorphism and appear more aggressive than cells from ρ0 tumours.
source: B16 melanoma cells form tumours in control mice (NS) showed prominent nuclear pleomorphism. They appeared more aggressive than cells from ρ0 tumours.
evidence: This is based on pathological examination of tumor sections.

claim: Tumours derived from B16 NDUFV1 KD and B16 SDHC KD cells show better histological differentiation associated with eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei and frequent deposits of melanin pigments, indicating the KD cells are less aggressive than their parental counterpart.
source: Tumours derived from both B16 NDUFV1 KD and B16 SDHC KD cells showed better histological differentiation associated with eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei and frequent deposits of melanin pigments, indicating the KD cells are less aggressive than their parental counterpart.
evidence: This is based on pathological examination of tumor sections, with interpretation about aggressiveness.

claim: Respiration recovery is essential for driving efficient tumour formation.
source: These data clearly point to respiration recovery as essential for driving efficient tumour formation, since suppression of respiration completely deregulated this process.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the knockdown experiments showing delayed or absent tumor formation.

claim: While with CII suppression the majority of mice formed tumours (albeit with additional lag time), most mice grafted with CI-compromised cells failed to form tumours within 100 days.
source: Interestingly, while with CII suppression the majority of mice formed tumours (albeit with additional lag time), most mice grafted with CI-compromised cells failed to form tumours within 100 days.
evidence: This is based on the tumor formation data from the knockdown experiments.

claim: Respiration is important for efficient tumour formation.
source: In summary, we show that respiration is important for efficient tumour formation, which is consistent with recent reports (Weinberg et al., 2010; Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The only plausible explanation for the acquisition of host mtDNA by tumor cells is the transfer of mtDNA from host cells to tumour cells with compromised mtDNA.
source: The only plausible explanation for this phenomenon is the transfer of mtDNA from host cells to tumour cells with compromised mtDNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NGS and sc/ddPCR data showing host origin of mtDNA.

claim: An attractive scenario is that whole mitochondria with their payload of mtDNA are transferred between cells.
source: An attractive scenario is that whole mitochondria with their payload of mtDNA are transferred, but alternative explanations such as cell fusion have also been suggested (Vitale et al., 2011; Maiuri and Kroemer, 2015).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis, with citation to alternative explanations.

claim: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been proposed as donors of mitochondria due to their high levels of Miro-1.
source: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been proposed as donors of mitochondria due to their high levels of Miro-1, which is the adaptor protein responsible for mitochondrial association with the microtubule mobility complex (Ahmad et al., 2014; Mills et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Miro-1 is the adaptor protein responsible for mitochondrial association with the microtubule mobility complex.
source: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been proposed as donors of mitochondria due to their high levels of Miro-1, which is the adaptor protein responsible for mitochondrial association with the microtubule mobility complex (Ahmad et al., 2014; Mills et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Miro-1 function, supported by citations.

claim: MitoDR stained mitochondria accumulate in CFSE stained B16ρ0 cells as a result of their transfer from MitoDR stained MSCs.
source: Representative images and quantitative evaluation (Figure 4A, Appendix 1—figure 3A,B) reveal accumulation of MitoDR stained mitochondria in CFSE stained ρ0 cells, as a result of their transfer from MitoDR stained MSCs.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and Appendix 1-figures 3A,B.

claim: Pairs of CFSE+B16 / MitoDR+MSC or CFSE+B16ρ0/MitoDR+B16 cells do not show evidence of MitoDR stained mitochondria in CFSE positive cells, excluding dye diffusion.
source: In similar experiments, pairs of either CFSE+B16 / MitoDR+MSC or CFSE+B16ρ0/MitoDR+B16 cells did not show any evidence of MitoDR stained mitochondria in CFSE positive cells, thereby excluding dye diffusion.
evidence: This is based on control co-culture experiments.

claim: Transfer of mitochondria between cells is a regulated process.
source: Collectively, this indicates that transfer of mitochondria between cells in a regulated process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-culture experiments showing selective transfer.

claim: DsRed mitochondria transfer from MSCs into recipient ρ0 cells via an intracellular bridge.
source: Appendix 1—figure 3C documents transfer of DsRed mitochondria from MSCs into the recipient ρ0 cells via an intracellular bridge.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Appendix 1-figure 3C.

claim: Double-positive (DP) cells with both red and blue fluorescence were found with a frequency of 0.23 ± 0.18 in the BFP-positive population.
source: Several days later, mice were sacrificed, the pre-tumour lesion excised, and single cell suspension sorted for double-positive (DP) cells with both red and blue fluorescence that on average were found with the frequency of 0.23 ± 0.18 in the BFP-positive population.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry sorting data from the in vivo experiment.

claim: Mouse stromal cells are a source of mitochondria that move into grafted B16ρ0 cells.
source: Figure 4B shows an image of a B16ρ0 DP cell prepared from a day 11 pre-tumour lesion, identifying mouse stromal cells as a source of mitochondria that moved into a grafted B16ρ0 cell.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: B16ρ0 DP cells contain fully formed mitochondrial cristae.
source: B16, B16ρ0, and B16ρ0 DP cells were subjected to transmission electron microscopy and STED microscopy to show the presence of fully formed mitochondrial cristae (Figure 4C) and mtDNA nucleoids in DP cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: B16ρ0 DP cells contain mtDNA nucleoids.
source: B16, B16ρ0, and B16ρ0 DP cells were subjected to transmission electron microscopy and STED microscopy to show the presence of fully formed mitochondrial cristae (Figure 4C) and mtDNA nucleoids in DP cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: B16ρ0 DP cells show strong binding of POLG1 to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA.
source: DP cells also showed strong binding of POLG1 to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA (Figure 4E) as well as recovery of respiration (Figure 4F), and showed a propensity to form tumours without a lag phase (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by mitoChIP data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: B16ρ0 DP cells show recovery of respiration.
source: DP cells also showed strong binding of POLG1 to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA (Figure 4E) as well as recovery of respiration (Figure 4F), and showed a propensity to form tumours without a lag phase (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by respiration data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: B16ρ0 DP cells show a propensity to form tumours without a lag phase.
source: DP cells also showed strong binding of POLG1 to the D-LOOP region of mtDNA (Figure 4E) as well as recovery of respiration (Figure 4F), and showed a propensity to form tumours without a lag phase (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by tumor formation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: mtDNA is transferred from stromal cells to B16ρ0 cells within intact mitochondria, resulting in the restoration of respiration and in efficient tumour formation.
source: These results document that mtDNA is transferred from stromal cells to B16ρ0 cells within intact mitochondria, resulting in the restoration of respiration and in efficient tumour formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DP cell experiments showing mitochondrial transfer, respiration recovery, and tumor formation.

claim: Horizontal gene transfer had not been known in mammals until recently.
source: Horizontal gene transfer is a process that until recently had not been known in mammals (Keeling and Palmer, 2008), but has been described for lower eukaryotes (Gladyshev et al., 2008), affecting their phenotype (Boschetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Horizontal gene transfer has been described for lower eukaryotes, affecting their phenotype.
source: Horizontal gene transfer is a process that until recently had not been known in mammals (Keeling and Palmer, 2008), but has been described for lower eukaryotes (Gladyshev et al., 2008), affecting their phenotype (Boschetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Mitochondrial gene transfer has been inferred in a 10,000 year-old canine transmissible venereal tumour (CTVT).
source: In mammals, the mitochondrial gene transfer has been inferred in a 10,000 year-old canine transmissible venereal tumour (CTVT) (Rebbeck et al., 2011; Murchison et al., 2014; Strakova and Murchison, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: A recent study showed at least 5 mtDNA transfers in CTVT within the last 1–2 thousand years.
source: These predictions have now been confirmed, and a recent study showed at least 5 mtDNA transfers in CTVT within the last 1–2 thousand years (Strakova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strakova et al., 2016.

claim: Mitochondrial transfer was reported in vitro with functional consequences.
source: Mitochondrial transfer was reported in vitro with functional consequences (Spees et al., 2006; Wang and Gerdes, 2015), as well as in mice with endogenously injected MSCs (Islam et al., 2012; Ahmad et al., 2014), but these results could also be explained by the association of membrane-bound particles or exosomes containing mitochondria with the damaged cells rather than functional mitochondria proliferating/dividing inside cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations, but the authors note alternative explanations.

claim: Tan et al. (2015) showed horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes between mammalian cells in vivo for the first time, based on acquisition of host mtDNA by ρ0 tumour cells.
source: A recent publication from our laboratory showed, for the first time, horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes between mammalian cells in vivo, based on acquisition of host mtDNA by ρ0 tumour cells and on the presence of host mtDNA markers in cell lines derived from these tumours (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: Several recently published papers provide evidence for horizontal transfer of mitochondria under (patho)physiological conditions.

claim: B16ρ0 cells do not form tumours unless they acquire mtDNA.
source: To address these queries, B16 metastatic melanoma cells without mtDNA and with compromised respiratory function were used. We show that B16ρ0 cells do not form tumours unless they acquire mtDNA and that severe suppression of either CI- or CII-dependent respiration leads to impaired ability to form tumours, directly linking mitochondrial respiration and tumor growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing delayed tumor formation from B16ρ0 cells.

claim: Severe suppression of either CI- or CII-dependent respiration leads to impaired ability to form tumours, directly linking mitochondrial respiration and tumor growth.

claim: CI is essential for respirasome assembly.
source: From a mechanistic point of view, CI is essential for respirasome assembly (Moreno-Lastres et al., 2012) that is needed for CI-dependent respiration (Acín-Pérez et al., 2008; Lapuente-Brun et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The respirasome is needed for CI-dependent respiration.

evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Tumours derived from B16ρ0 cells feature much higher CI-dependent respiration than tumours from B16 cells.
source: Another indication of the importance of CI is the finding that tumours derived from B16ρ0 cells feature much higher CI-dependent respiration (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by respiration data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Primary tumour-derived B16ρ0SC cells feature a fully assembled respirasome and complete recovery of respiration.
source: We document here that the primary tumour-derived B16ρ0SC cells feature a fully assembled respirasome and complete recovery of respiration, while corresponding 4T1ρ0SC cells show only partial (20–25%) recovery of respiration (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on data in the manuscript and comparison to previous work.

claim: 4T1ρ0SC cells show only partial (20–25%) recovery of respiration.
source: We document here that the primary tumour-derived B16ρ0SC cells feature a fully assembled respirasome and complete recovery of respiration, while corresponding 4T1ρ0SC cells show only partial (20–25%) recovery of respiration (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to data from the authors' previous work.

claim: 4T1ρ0SC cells formed tumours with a longer delay than parental 4T1 cells.
source: Consistent with this, 4T1ρ0SC cells formed tumours with a longer delay than parental 4T1 cells, while no delay was observed for B16ρ0SC cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tumor formation data between the two cell types.

claim: No delay in tumor formation was observed for B16ρ0SC cells compared to parental B16 cells.
source: Consistent with this, 4T1ρ0SC cells formed tumours with a longer delay than parental 4T1 cells, while no delay was observed for B16ρ0SC cells.
evidence: This is based on tumor formation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: B16ρ0 cells have a higher requirement for respiration recovery to form tumours than 4T1ρ0 cells.
source: This is likely related to the higher requirement of B16ρ0 cells for respiration recovery to form tumours.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between B16 and 4T1 cells.

claim: B16 cells have routine respiration of some 100 pmol O2/s/106 cells.
source: This 'threshold', apparently lower for 4T1ρ0 cells, may be due to higher routine respiration of B16 cells of some 100 pmol O2/s/106 cells (Figure 1E) when compared to less than 20 pmol O2/s/106 cells for 4T1 cells (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on respiration data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 4T1 cells have routine respiration of less than 20 pmol O2/s/106 cells.

evidence: This refers to data from the authors' previous work.

claim: The transient nature of dsRed expression in recipient B16ρ0 cell mitochondria in the in vivo model sheds light on the mechanism of mitochondrial transfer.
source: The transient nature of dsRed expression in recipient B16ρ0 cell mitochondria in the in vivo model sheds additional light on the mechanism of mitochondrial transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that red fluorescence is lost over time.

claim: When dsRed-containing mitochondria are selectively transferred from the host into the recipient cells, dsRed cannot be replenished in the donated mitochondria by de novo synthesis.
source: When dsRed-containing mitochondria are selectively transferred from the host into the recipient cells, dsRed cannot be replenished in the donated mitochondria by de novo synthesis (not being encoded in the recipient's nuclear genome), and the red fluorescence in donated mitochondria is quickly lost.
evidence: This is logical inference based on the genetic system used.

claim: If cell fusion were responsible for the observed acquisition of mitochondria from the donor cells, the donor's nuclear material would also be transferred, and mitochondrial dsRed expression would be maintained.
source: On the other hand, if cell fusion were responsible for the observed acquisition of mitochondria from the donor cells (Maiuri and Kroemer, 2015), the donor's nuclear material would also be transferred, and mitochondrial dsRed expression would be maintained.
evidence: This is logical inference used to rule out cell fusion as the mechanism.

claim: The selective transfer of whole, intact mitochondria is the only possible explanation for the observed acquisition of mitochondria from donor cells.
source: As this is not the case, the selective transfer of whole, intact mitochondria remains the only possible explanation of our experimental data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dsRed expression data and logical reasoning.

claim: Tunnelling nanotubes are a plausible mode of intercellular transfer of mitochondria.
source: The next step will be to investigate the mechanism of mitochondrial trafficking between cells in vivo, with tunnelling nanotubes being a plausible mode of intercellular transfer of the organelles (Rustom et al., 2004; Rogers and Bhattacharya, 2014; Rustom, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions, supported by citations.

claim: Recovery of respiration in tumor cells with damaged mtDNA is essential for efficient tumour formation.
source: We conclude that recovery of respiration in tumor cells with damaged mtDNA is essential for efficient tumour formation and that this is accomplished by the intercellular transfer of whole mitochondria.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, based on all the experimental data.

claim: Recovery of respiration in tumor cells with damaged mtDNA is accomplished by the intercellular transfer of whole mitochondria.
source: We conclude that recovery of respiration in tumor cells with damaged mtDNA is essential for efficient tumour formation and that this is accomplished by the intercellular transfer of whole mitochondria.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, based on all the experimental data.

claim: The findings are consistent with the emerging notion of the essential role of respiration in cancer cell proliferation and tumor progression.
source: Our findings are consistent with the emerging notion of the essential role of respiration in cancer cell proliferation and tumor progression (LeBleu et al., 2014; Viale et al., 2014; Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015; Cardaci et al., 2015; Lussey-Lepoutre et al., 2015; Berridge et al., 2015; Viale et al., 2015), and of a role for mitochondrial transfer in maintaining the bioenergetics balance (Sinha et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This places the findings in the context of recent literature.

claim: Mitochondrial transfer plays a role in maintaining the bioenergetics balance.

evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Recent studies on horizontal mitochondrial transfer indicate two novel approaches to cancer therapy: targeting mitochondrial respiration and blocking transfer of mitochondria from stromal cells to cancer cells.
source: From translational angle, recent studies on horizontal mitochondrial transfer indicate two tantalising, novel approaches to cancer therapy: targeting mitochondrial respiration and blocking transfer of mitochondria from stromal cells to cancer cells.
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic implications based on the findings.

claim: This paper is the first report to show lasting functional consequences of a well-documented mitochondrial transfer event.
source: Finally, to the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first report to show lasting functional consequences of a well-documented mitochondrial transfer event.
evidence: This is the authors' claim about the novelty of their work.
